# VISION.md

The shared charter for every agent working on this project. An identical copy
sits at the root of every repository; the copy in the site repository
(`blakeaaronroberts.github.io`) is canonical. Every repository's `CLAUDE.md`
points here. If a repo's local instructions disagree with this file, stop and
tell Blake.

**Do not edit this file.** Only the Steward writes it, and only with Blake's
approval. Its history is in `VISION_CHANGELOG.md`.

Status: v2, approved by Blake 2026-11-14. Last updated 2026-11-14.
Interim code name: Rising Edge (placeholder).

## 1. Vision

ECE is taught with static pictures of dynamic things. This project is a free,
open suite of tools for teaching 200–600 level electrical and computer
engineering in which **a concept is defined once and rendered everywhere**.

A concept (a full adder, a state machine, an RC filter) is described once as a
precise, executable source: a circuit, its parameters and the simulation that
governs it. From that source the suite produces a textbook-quality figure, an
animation, a slide, a browser interactive, practice problems and a lab check.
Because every form comes from one source, they agree; because motion is driven
by real simulation, the visuals never lie.

Every capability is also a small standalone web tool: nothing to install, one
job each, shared model and style, clean exports, and the ability to pass its
output to the other tools.

The suite starts with digital logic and grows into the analog domain.

Non-goals: not a learning management system, no AI features for students, not a
commercial product, not a replacement for the instructor.

## 2. Principles

- Visual intuition: show the mechanism.
- Active learning: students predict, manipulate, check.
- Real hardware: theory always lands on something physical.
- Industry relevance: the tools and workflows working engineers use.
- One source, many outputs; never redraw the same concept twice.
- One tool, one job; every tool usable on its own and connectable to the others.
- Small, consistent, documented modules Blake can learn to build himself.
- Finished beats sprawling. Polish one piece before starting the next.
- Token-conscious: spend inference on judgement, never on repetition.

## 3. Constraints

- **Employer-agnostic.** No institution names, brand names, brand-colour names,
  work emails or work paths in code, identifiers, file or folder names.
  Institution branding exists only as a private theme.
- **Privacy and FERPA.** No student data in any repository or hosted page.
  Tools run in the browser and store nothing about students on a server.
  Anything that touches grades or lab results keeps them in the institution's
  own systems (exports go there, never the reverse), and no AI tool processes
  identifiable student records.
- **Free and open-source tools only, or our own.** Everything used to build, run
  or view the suite is free and open-source software (fonts included) or our
  own. Free hosting and CI are replaceable conveniences; every build runs on any
  Linux machine. AI agents help write the suite; nothing in it depends on them.
  Record each dependency's licence in that repo's `DECISIONS.md`.
- **Clean IP, both doors open** (Blake, 2026-11-14). The work must be releasable
  as open source and transferable to a university. So: only dependencies with
  licences compatible with both; nothing copied from textbooks, standards (e.g.
  IEEE 1800), papers or other courses: our own text, figures and examples,
  citing sources by clause or page; clean authorship records in git. No LICENSE
  file, licence header or badge until Blake decides ownership and licence; a
  licence grant cannot be withdrawn.
- **Windows-first** locally; **browser-first** for public tools.
- **Static hosting.** Tools run in the browser (JavaScript, WebAssembly) or
  serve prebuilt outputs. Anything needing a server is a separate service with
  the trade-off written down.
- **Approval.** Blake signs off on anything students or the public see, except
  READMEs (the Scribe approves them). Agents write "approved" only when Blake
  directly says so for the items he names.

## 4. Architecture

Four layers; everything above layer 2 depends only on the core model.

1. **Sources.** Symbols, KiCad schematics, HDL, SPICE netlists, Boolean
   expressions, parameters.
2. **Core model.** Circuits, Boolean functions, signals over time, simulation,
   one style system with swappable themes. Renderer-independent; never imports
   Manim or any drawing library.
3. **Renderers.** Static figures, animations, slides, web interactives, problem
   generators, lab checks.
4. **Products.** Figure Editor (with its Timing pane), the standalone tools,
   Explorations, Practice, Labs, the reference sites.

### Modules and interfaces

Each repository is a standalone module with its own builder. Modules connect
only through versioned file formats, pinned by release tag; no module imports
another repository's code directly.

| Format | What it carries |
|---|---|
| `circuit` | Elements, pins, nets, wire routes, parameters, drawing annotations, figure style |
| Symbol pack | Each approved element as SVG plus pin and grid data, per line weight and theme |
| `scenario` | Inputs over time: the steps of an animation or a timing diagram |
| `trace` | Every net's value at every step, produced by a simulator |
| SystemVerilog | Source text in, source text out: import to a `circuit` (and `scenario`), export from a `circuit`; the language itself is the interface, handled by open-source front ends |
| `function` | A Boolean function: truth table, expressions (SOP, POS, minimised), variable names |

Every tool reads and writes these formats, so any output can be sent to another
tool: a K-map's minimised expression becomes a circuit; a circuit's simulation
becomes a timing diagram, frames and an animation; a trace drives a Manim
render in the animation library.

### Simulation

Simulation produces traces from circuits and scenarios; no renderer invents
behaviour. First, four-valued logic (0, 1, X, Z), zero delay by default, integer
delays as an option. SystemVerilog arrives with it: the simulator runs the circuit, and the
SystemVerilog import and export described in Phase 1 use proven open-source front
ends and engines. Then analog (SPICE-class) simulation,
using proven open-source engines compiled to run in the browser where that is
practical, unless the engine research memo shows a better path. We do not write
our own Verilator or SPICE.

## 5. Repository map

| Repository | Role | Visibility |
|---|---|---|
| `blakeaaronroberts.github.io` | Quarto site: the suite's public home, tools, explorations, reference pages, this file | Public |
| `manimations` | Animation library and circuit toolbox (CircuiTikZ symbols, Manim motion), symbol pack export, animations rendered from traces | Private |
| `circuit-model` | Core model: formats, schemas, symbol packs, simulator, importers, Boolean-function library | Private until Blake decides licence and ownership |

Do not create new repositories without Blake's say-so.

## 6. Phases and goals

**Phase 0, Foundation** (done): toolbox core, style and themes, circuit schema,
symbol pack, first Figure Editor.

**Phase 1, Proving ground** (now; year-one success): one digital logic course
done end to end, and a public site with a polished set of tools and
explorations. In order:

1. **Figure Editor complete for Harris and Harris chapters 1 to 5.** One stable
   tool with a minimisable Timing pane (also a standalone page), slide export
   with layouts, frames with a frame window or playhead, N-input variants, the
   expanded symbol set, and animation export.
2. **Simulation underneath:** `scenario`, `trace` and the four-valued simulator,
   so timing diagrams, frames and animations come from real simulation. The
   finished editor and simulator also speak SystemVerilog (the synthesizable
   subset taught in the course): import a module to get a schematic, its
   hierarchy and a timing diagram from a testbench or scenario; export a
   circuit as a SystemVerilog module and testbench. Round trip first, then
   wider language coverage.
3. **Small tools, shipped fast:** truth table, K-map, SOP and POS, Boolean
   step-by-step solver, number systems, and the core equation library
   (100–300 level, each with explanation and graph).
4. **First flagship:** the 4-bit ripple-carry adder as figure, animation and
   interactive from one file.
5. **Site launch:** once the flagship and a project page exist; until then the
   home page is a landing page and other pages are unlisted and `noindex`.
6. **The course run:** all figures, animations and slides for the course.

**Phase 2, Interaction:** practice and autograding with export to any LMS
(Common Cartridge), full-language SystemVerilog in the browser and the SystemVerilog
reference site, the wider equation library (to 600 level), more explorations.

**Phase 3, Hardware and analog:** remote FPGA lab (teaching, upper-division
courses and research uses), analog simulation, logic-analyser bridge,
datasheet delays, other course areas.

**Phase 4, Adoption:** adoption kit, other instructors and institutions,
published results.

Research memos (decisions, no code) may run ahead of their phase.

## 7. Shared conventions

### Style system
- One settings file per repo defines colours, line weights, sizes, grid and
  fonts; everything else reads it or is generated from it.
- Colours are referenced by role (ink, low, high, unknown, floating, flow,
  accent, background), never by hue or brand. A user's chosen level colours may
  be saved in a figure as role overrides.
- **Default theme:** Okabe-Ito (`high` is vermillion, #D55E00), regular weight.
  Defaults, galleries and committed renders always use it; editor exports do
  unless the user chooses otherwise. A public `dark` theme may be offered and
  passes the same colour-blind and contrast checks. Line weight is one of thin,
  regular or bold per figure, drawn by the toolbox, never scaled.
- **Maths is STIX Two everywhere.** LaTeX outputs: STIX Two Math and Text,
  Fira Mono for element names. Site and web tools: MathJax 4 with its pinned
  `mathjax-stix2` bundle. Exported figures use outlined glyphs.
- Private themes live in a git-ignored folder; never commit one.
- All on-screen words in figures go through LaTeX or MathJax.
- Colour-blind safe palettes; in web tools signal state never relies on colour
  alone.

### Language
Kind, inclusive, current terms (leader/follower, controller/peripheral,
allowlist/denylist, `main`); mention an older term once where students need to
recognise it. Student-facing text never says "simply", "obviously" or
"trivially".

### Approval gates
Everything starts as a draft (READMEs excepted). Only Blake approves. Circuits
and public pages use approved elements only; new needs become drafts for
review. Look at your own render before handing work over.

### Documentation
Every repo has a `README.md`, a `CLAUDE.md` pointing here, a `DECISIONS.md`
(date, decision, reason) and a HOW_TO for each extension point, updated in the
same change that alters the pattern.

### Testing and CI
Tests cover the core model first. CI renders every approved element and example
and compares against references, on a free Linux runner.

### Tokens
- Prompts name a batch and state its intent in a few lines; the handoff holds
  the details. Never re-paste a spec.
- Handoff files keep only open and recent batches; finished ones move to
  `docs/handoff-archive.md`.
- Checks match the change: small changes get a test run and one screenshot;
  the 4x zoom is for new geometry.
- Reviewers read what changed since their last run, plus one rotating area.

### Prompts between agents
Every prompt any agent writes for another states: the model and effort level,
the intent in plain words, the batch or files, scope limits, mandatory checks,
and where to stop.

## 8. How work flows

- **Blake** talks to each agent directly and starts batches by name.
- **Steward** (architect chat): reads all repos and reports to Blake. Writes
  only `VISION.md`, `VISION_CHANGELOG.md`, each repo's `docs/STEWARD_HANDOFF.md`
  and `docs/handoff-archive.md`, and research memos in `proposals/`, all with
  Blake's approval (the Current state block needs none).
- **Builders**, one per repository: do the batch Blake names, update its Status
  and notes, ship a README stub with each new module.
- **Scribe**: owns documentation (READMEs, `docs/`, HOW_TO guides), never code
  or config. Writes builder requests in `docs/SCRIBE_HANDOFF.md`; tracks its
  work in `docs/SCRIBE_TODO.md`; may commit docs to `main`. Public pages stay
  drafts until Blake approves.
- **Reviewers** (Security, Engineer, Code Review, Aesthetic, IP Inspector):
  report-only, weekly, reading changes since their last run plus one rotating
  deep area. Each writes only `reviews/<agent>.md` in the repos it reviews, top
  10 findings ranked. The IP Inspector checks licences, attribution and copied
  material. The Steward triages findings into batches for Blake.
- **Sync.** Blake types `sync`. The Steward refreshes each handoff's Current
  state block (facts only) and the tracker; every other agent pulls, reads the
  Current state block, this file, its `CLAUDE.md` and the handoffs, lets the
  files win over its memory, and replies in five lines or fewer.
- Plan first for architecture; build in batches with review stops; prefer the
  smallest change that moves a current goal.

## 9. Open decisions (do not assume an answer)

- Ownership and licence (both doors open, section 3).
- The suite's real name.
- Engines for SystemVerilog import, simulation and analog (research memo; decides the front end and the browser route).
- FERPA confirmation against the institution's own guidance (research memo).
